title: A Red, Red Rose
author: Robert Burns
fullContent:
O my Luve is like a red, red rose
That’s newly sprung in June;
O my Luve is like the melody
That’s sweetly played in tune.

So fair art thou, my bonnie lass,
So deep in luve am I;
And I will luve thee still, my dear,
Till a’ the seas gang dry.

Till a’ the seas gang dry, my dear,
And the rocks melt wi’ the sun;
I will love thee still, my dear,
While the sands o’ life shall run.

And fare thee weel, my only luve!
And fare thee weel awhile!
And I will come again, my luve,
Though it were ten thousand mile.
litchartsAnalysis: The poem navigates the tension between fleeting physical beauty and eternal devotion through hyperbolic, geological metaphors of endurance. It asserts that while youthful allure is inherently transient, the profound emotional bond it sparks transcends physical decay and mortal limits.
historicalContext:
Composed in 1794 during the early Romantic period, the lyric reflects the era's focus on intense emotion and pastoral naturalism.
Robert Burns crafted the work in Anglo-Scots as part of his project to preserve and elevate traditional Scottish folk ballads.

title: Ode to the West Wind
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
fullContent:
I
O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn's being,
Thou, from whose unseen presence the leaves dead
Are driven, like ghosts from an enchanter fleeing,

Yellow, and black, and pale, and hectic red,
Pestilence-stricken multitudes: O thou,
Who chariotest to their dark wintry bed

The winged seeds, where they lie cold and low,
Each like a corpse within its grave, until
Thine azure sister of the Spring shall blow

Her clarion o'er the dreaming earth, and fill
(Driving sweet buds like flocks to feed in air)
With living hues and odours plain and hill:

Wild Spirit, which art moving everywhere;
Destroyer and preserver; hear, oh hear!

II
Thou on whose stream, mid the steep sky's commotion,
Loose clouds like earth's decaying leaves are shed,
Shook from the tangled boughs of Heaven and Ocean,

Angels of rain and lightning: there are spread
On the blue surface of thine aëry surge,
Like the bright hair uplifted from the head

Of some fierce Maenad, even from the dim verge
Of the horizon to the zenith's height,
The locks of the approaching storm. Thou dirge

Of the dying year, to which this closing night
Will be the dome of a vast sepulchre,
Vaulted with all thy congregated might

Of vapours, from whose solid atmosphere
Black rain, and fire, and hail will burst: oh hear!

III
Thou who didst waken from his summer dreams
The blue Mediterranean, where he lay,
Lull'd by the coil of his crystalline streams,

Beside a pumice isle in Baiae's bay,
And saw in sleep old palaces and towers
Quivering within the wave's intenser day,

All overgrown with azure moss and flowers
So sweet, the sense faints picturing them! Thou
For whose path the Atlantic's level powers

Cleave themselves into chasms, while far below
The sea-blooms and the oozy woods which wear
The sapless foliage of the ocean, know

Thy voice, and suddenly grow gray with fear,
And tremble and despoil themselves: oh hear!

IV
If I were a dead leaf thou mightest bear;
If I were a swift cloud to fly with thee;
A wave to pant beneath thy power, and share

The impulse of thy strength, only less free
Than thou, O uncontrollable! If even
I were as in my boyhood, and could be

The comrade of thy wanderings over Heaven,
As then, when to outstrip thy skiey speed
Scarce seem'd a vision; I would ne'er have striven

As thus with thee in prayer in my sore need.
Oh, lift me as a wave, a leaf, a cloud!
I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!

A heavy weight of hours has chain'd and bow'd
One too like thee: tameless, and swift, and proud.

V
Make me thy lyre, even as the forest is:
What if my leaves are falling like its own!
The tumult of thy mighty harmonies

Will take from both a deep, autumnal tone,
Sweet though in sadness. Be thou, Spirit fierce,
My spirit! Be thou me, impetuous one!

Drive my dead thoughts over the universe
Like wither'd leaves to quicken a new birth!
And, by the incantation of this verse,

Scatter, as from an unextinguish'd hearth
Ashes and sparks, my words among mankind!
Be through my lips to unawaken'd earth

The trumpet of a prophecy! O Wind,
If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?
litchartsAnalysis: The ode dramatizes the paradox of natural destruction as an indispensable prerequisite for revolutionary creative and spiritual rebirth. Shelley posits the poet not as an isolated creator, but as a prophetic instrument whose decaying mortality must be violently dispersed to awaken human consciousness.
historicalContext:
Written in 1819 near Florence during the British Romantic era, the poem was published in 1820 alongside Prometheus Unbound.
Shelley was galvanized by political stagnation in post-Napoleonic Europe and the Peterloo Massacre, channeling natural tempest into a call for social regeneration.

title: The Lamb
author: William Blake
fullContent:
Little Lamb who made thee
Dost thou know who made thee
Gave thee life & bid thee feed.
By the stream & o'er the mead;
Gave thee clothing of delight,
Softest clothing wooly bright;
Gave thee such a tender voice,
Making all the vales rejoice!
Little Lamb who made thee
Dost thou know who made thee

Little Lamb I'll tell thee,
Little Lamb I'll tell thee!
He is called by thy name,
For he calls himself a Lamb:
He is meek & he is mild,
He became a little child:
I a child & thou a lamb,
We are called by his name.
Little Lamb God bless thee.
Little Lamb God bless thee.
litchartsAnalysis: Through a catechismal dialogue between an innocent child and a lamb, the poem posits that the creator, natural world, and humanity share a single unified essence. It argues that childhood innocence offers an uncorrupted metaphysical insight into divine grace that adult rationalism obscures.
historicalContext:
Published in 1789 at the dawn of British Romanticism, the poem appeared as an integral centerpiece of William Blake's illuminated collection Songs of Innocence.
Written amid the rise of the Industrial Revolution, Blake crafted this pastoral vision to contrast emerging urban degradation with uncorrupted spiritual purity.

title: The Chimney Sweeper
author: William Blake
fullContent:
When my mother died I was very young,
And my father sold me while yet my tongue
Could scarcely cry "weep! weep! weep! weep!"
So your chimneys I sweep & in soot I sleep.

There's little Tom Dacre, who cried when his head
That curled like a lamb's back, was shaved, so I said,
"Hush, Tom! never mind it, for when your head's bare,
You know that the soot cannot spoil your white hair."

And so he was quiet, & that very night,
As Tom was a-sleeping he had such a sight!
That thousands of sweepers, Dick, Joe, Ned, & Jack,
Were all of them locked up in coffins of black;

And by came an Angel who had a bright key,
And he opened the coffins & set them all free;
Then down a green plain, leaping, laughing they run,
And wash in a river and shine in the Sun.

Then naked & white, all their bags left behind,
They rise upon clouds, and sport in the wind.
And the Angel told Tom, if he'd be a good boy,
He'd have God for his father & never want joy.

And so Tom awoke; and we rose in the dark
And got with our bags & our brushes to work.
Though the morning was cold, Tom was happy & warm;
So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.
litchartsAnalysis: Blake employs an irony-laden pastoral vision to dramatize how institutional religion placates marginalized children into tolerating lethal socio-economic exploitation. By framing moral docility as divine salvation, the verse exposes the cruel disparity between pastoral childhood ideals and systemic urban brutality.
historicalContext:
Published in 1789 as part of Songs of Innocence during the dawn of British Romanticism and the Industrial Revolution.
Blake was galvanized by the rampant, dangerous use of impoverished child labor across 18th-century London's urban chimneys.

title: The Tyger
author: William Blake
fullContent:
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies.
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp!

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?
litchartsAnalysis: The poem wrestles with the theological paradox of whether a benevolent deity could simultaneously author sublime terror and gentle innocence. Through relentless rhetorical interrogation, it frames creation as a perilous act of industrial and cosmic daring.
historicalContext:
Composed in 1794 during the British Romantic era as part of Songs of Innocence and of Experience.
Blake was heavily influenced by the rise of the Industrial Revolution and his own trade as a printmaker and engraver.

title: Robinson Crusoe
author: Daniel Defoe
fullContent:
Cast ashore as the sole survivor of a devastating shipwreck off an uncharted Caribbean island, Robinson Crusoe confronted the terrifying reality of complete isolation. Overcoming his initial despair, he salvaged provisions, gunpowder, and timber from the stranded vessel before the relentless sea swallowed its remains. He established a secure habitation against a rocky cliff, surrounding it with a sturdy turf wall, and erected a notched wooden cross to measure the passage of lonely days and preserve his connection to civil time.

Deprived of human fellowship, Crusoe turned his energies toward mastering his wild domain through ingenuity, rigorous discipline, and labor. He cultivated patches of salvaged barley and rice, tamed wild goats into manageable herds, and learned to bake bread and fashion crude clay pottery. A violent illness accompanied by a frightening fever-dream forced him into deep spiritual introspection, prompting him to repent his former rebellious wandering, embrace Christianity, and view the untamed island as a providential sanctuary removed from European vice.

The profound illusion of absolute solitary dominion shattered twenty-three years into his isolation when Crusoe discovered a single human footprint pressed into the sand. The discovery plunged him into profound terror, revealing that indigenous groups periodically visited the shores to perform cannibalistic rites. Balancing self-preservation with moral judgment, Crusoe maintained extreme vigilance until circumstance compelled him to ambush a group of captors, thereby rescuing a young native man whom he named Friday.

Crusoe established absolute authority over Friday, instructing him in English and Christian doctrine while training him as a faithful companion and servant. Together, they navigated further violent encounters with approaching natives, successfully rescuing Friday's father alongside a shipwrecked Spanish sailor. The island dynamic shifted definitively when an English vessel arrived, torn by mutiny; Crusoe outmaneuvered the mutineers, restored the rightful captain, and finally secured passage back to civilization after twenty-eight years of exile.
litchartsAnalysis: Defoe's novel articulates the rise of modern economic individualism and colonial dominion through Crusoe's calculated mastery over nature, providence, and indigenous bodies. It stages an ideological reconciliation between merchant capitalism and spiritual salvation, arguing that survival and moral redemption demand the rational subjugation of the wilderness.
historicalContext:
Published in 1719 during the early Augustan Age, the novel helped establish novelistic realism amidst the expansion of British mercantile imperialism.
Defoe drew primary biographical inspiration from the widely publicized real-life survival account of privateer Alexander Selkirk, marooned until 1711.

title: Ode to a Nightingale
author: John Keats
fullContent:
My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
    My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
    One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:
'Tis not through envy of thy happy lot,
    But being too happy in thine happiness,—
        That thou, light-winged Dryad of the trees
            In some melodious plot
    Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,
        Singest of summer in full-throated ease.

O, for a draught of vintage! that hath been
    Cool'd a long age in the deep-delved earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country green,
    Dance, and Provençal song, and sunburnt mirth!
O for a beaker full of the warm South,
    Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
        With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
            And purple-stained mouth;
    That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,
        And with thee fade away into the forest dim:

Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
    What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
    Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;
Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs,
    Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
        Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
            And leaden-eyed despairs,
    Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,
        Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
    Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
    Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:
Already with thee! tender is the night,
    And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
        Cluster'd around by all her starry Fays;
            But here there is no light,
    Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown
        Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways.

I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
    Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmed darkness, guess each sweet
    Wherewith the seasonable month endows
The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild;
    White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
        Fast fading violets cover'd up in leaves;
            And mid-May's eldest child,
    The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,
        The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves.

Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
    I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call'd him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
    To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
    To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
        While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
            In such an ecstasy!
    Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
        To thy high requiem become a sod.

Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
    No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
    In ancient days by emperor and clown:
Perhaps the self-same song that found a path
    Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
        She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
            The same that oft-times hath
    Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam
        Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.

Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
    To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the fancy cannot cheat so well
    As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf.
Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades
    Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
        Up the hill-side; and now 'tis buried deep
            In the next valley-glades:
    Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
        Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?
litchartsAnalysis: The ode dramatizes the agonized tension between mortal suffering and the transcendent immortality of creative beauty. Keats demonstrates that while poetic imagination briefly bridges the void of human grief, conscious reality inevitably collapses the visionary trance.
historicalContext: Written in the spring of 1819 during the height of the English Romantic movement. Composed in a Hampstead garden shortly after Keats nursed his brother Tom through a fatal bout of tuberculosis.

title: Gulliver's Travels
author: Jonathan Swift
fullContent:
Lemuel Gulliver begins his voyages as an inquisitive English surgeon eager to explore distant lands, only to find himself shipwrecked on the shores of Lilliput. Bound by thousands of tiny threads, he awakens into captivity among a miniature civilization measuring mere inches in height. Though the diminutive king grants Gulliver liberty after exacting strict oaths of allegiance, the grandeur of the court soon reveals itself as petty cruelty and tyrannical ambition. When Gulliver heroically neutralizes the neighboring fleet of Blefuscu yet refuses to aid in their complete enslavement, the ungrateful Lilliputian monarch secretly sentences him to be blinded for treason, compelling Gulliver to escape abroad.

Setting out once more, Gulliver is abandoned in Brobdingnag, where the physical scale reverses and he experiences the vulnerability of an insect among towering giants. Exhibited for profit as an exhausted carnival oddity by a rapacious farmer, he is eventually bought by the Queen and given refuge, though subjected to constant domestic dangers and court ridicule. Desperate to assert the dignity of European civilization, Gulliver offers the Brobdingnagian king the destructive secret of gunpowder, but the enlightened ruler recoils in horror, dismissing humanity as the most pernicious race of odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the earth.

His third journey casts him onto the floating island of Laputa and the mainland of Lagado, whose elite live entirely engrossed in theoretical mathematics, music, and astronomy. Blind to common sense, these detached intellectuals leave their actual lands in ruin while patronizing an academy of projectors who squander public resources on futile experiments like extracting sunbeams from cucumbers. Confronted by historical ghosts and decrepit immortals across neighboring islands, Gulliver witnesses how pedantic hubris and the vanity of mortal wisdom systematically dismantle practical human happiness.

In his final voyage, stranded after a crew mutiny, Gulliver encounters the Houyhnhnms, a race of noble, rational horses who master the bestial, degenerate humanoids known as Yahoos. Enamored by the equines' peaceful society and absence of falsehood, Gulliver seeks to erase his own human identity, yet he is recognized as fundamentally identical to the vile Yahoos he despises. Banished from their utopian land and forcibly escorted back to Europe, he ends his travels permanently alienated from mankind, revolted by his family's touch and seeking solace solely in the company of stable horses.
litchartsAnalysis: Through a relentless inversion of physical and moral scale, Swift dismantles the Enlightenment conceit of human rational supremacy by exposing European institutions as inherently petty, hypocritical, and savage. Gulliver’s eventual descent into misanthropy illustrates the devastating cost of total relativism, trapping him in profound alienation between an unattainable ideal of pure reason and the inescapable depravity of human nature.
historicalContext:
Published in 1726 during the Augustan age, the novel reflects bitter partisan conflicts between Tories and Whigs following the 1714 accession of King George I.
Exiled to Dublin and energized by the Scriblerus Club, Swift subverted popular colonial travel narratives to satirize imperial pride and intellectual vanity.
